title: Magnetic Hysteresis
short_intro: Hysteresis is the lagging of magnetic induction (B) behind the magnetizing field intensity (H) when a ferromagnetic material is subjected to a cyclic magnetizing process. This phenomenon results in energy dissipation per cycle equal to the area of the B-H loop.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of magnetic hysteresis, B-H curve, retention, coercivity, and core selection criteria for transformers and electromagnets.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantitative calculation of hysteresis energy loss per unit volume per cycle, comparison of soft and hard magnetic materials, and application in alternating current circuits.

prerequisites: Magnetic field intensity (H) and magnetic induction (B)
Intensity of magnetization (I) and magnetic susceptibility

concept_notes.heading: B-H Loop (Hysteresis Loop)
bullets: When a ferromagnetic specimen is taken through a complete cycle of magnetization, the curve of B versus H forms a closed loop known as the hysteresis loop.
The non-linear path reflects the irreversible domain wall motion and domain rotation under the influence of an external magnetic field.
The loop exhibits rotational symmetry about the origin for symmetric cyclic magnetization.

concept_notes.heading: Remanence and Coercivity
bullets: Retentivity (or Remanence, B_r): The value of magnetic induction B left in the material when the magnetizing field H is reduced to zero from saturation.
Coercivity (H_c): The magnitude of the reverse magnetizing field required to reduce the residual magnetic induction B to zero.
Materials with high retentivity and high coercivity are termed hard magnetic materials, while those with low retentivity and low coercivity are soft magnetic materials.

concept_notes.heading: Hysteresis Loss
bullets: Work done per unit volume in taking a ferromagnetic material through one complete cycle of magnetization is equal to the area enclosed by the B-H loop.
The energy lost per unit volume per cycle is given by the integral W = oint H dB.
This dissipated energy appears as thermal energy (heat) in magnetic cores of transformers, generators, and inductors.

concept_notes.heading: Soft versus Hard Ferromagnetic Materials
bullets: Soft Magnetic Materials (e.g., Soft Iron, Permalloy): Narrow hysteresis loop, low coercivity, low hysteresis loss, high initial permeability, used in transformer cores and electromagnets.
Hard Magnetic Materials (e.g., Alnico, Neodymium-Iron-Boron): Wide hysteresis loop, high retentivity, high coercivity, used for making permanent magnets.
The choice of material depends strictly on minimizing core losses in AC machinery or maximizing permanent retention in transducers.

derivations.title: Work Done per Unit Volume in Magnetization
derivations.conditions: Quasi-static cyclic magnetization of a ferromagnetic material
steps: Consider a solenoid of n turns per unit length carrying current I, producing a magnetic field intensity H = nI.
When current changes by dI, the induced electromotive force in the coil opposes the change, and the work done dW per unit volume against this back emf in time dt is given by dW = H dB.
Integrating over a complete cycle of magnetization to find the total work done (energy loss) per unit volume: W = oint dW = oint H dB.
derivations.result: W = oint H dB, which represents the area of the B-H loop.

derivations.title: Steinmetz Empirical Formula for Hysteresis Power Loss
derivations.conditions: Ferromagnetic core subjected to an alternating magnetic field of frequency f
steps: Empirical observation shows that the area of the hysteresis loop depends on the maximum flux density B_{max} raised to a power alpha, known as the Steinmetz coefficient (typically between 1.6 and 2.0).
Energy loss per unit volume per cycle is expressed as W_h = eta B_{max}^{alpha}, where eta is the material-dependent Steinmetz constant.
If the alternating field operates at a frequency f, the power loss per unit volume P_h is the energy loss per cycle multiplied by the frequency.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Standard B-H Hysteresis Loop
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A closed, centrally symmetric loop plotting B (y-axis) against H (x-axis), indicating saturation point, retentivity on the B-axis, and coercivity on the H-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the non-linear multi-valued relation between B and H, illustrating residual magnetism and energy dissipation per cycle.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct identification of retentivity, coercivity, and calculation of hysteresis energy loss from loop area.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Comparison of Soft Iron and Steel Hysteresis Loops
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two loops on the same axes: Soft iron with a tall, narrow loop (high B_r, very low H_c); Steel with a shorter, wider loop (moderate B_r, high H_c).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Soft iron loses magnetization easily and has minimal area (low loss), whereas steel retains magnetization strongly (high coercivity).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions matching core material properties with appropriate engineering applications (transformers vs permanent magnets).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Ballistic Galvanometer / Fluxmeter Experimental Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A toroidal specimen wound with primary and secondary coils connected to a variable DC source, reversing switch, and a ballistic galvanometer.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used experimentally to map the B-H curve point-by-point by measuring induced charge flow upon field reversal.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: VIVA and conceptual questions regarding experimental determination of magnetic induction B.

solved_numericals.question: The area of a B-H hysteresis loop for a given ferromagnetic material is equivalent to 250 J/m^3. If the core volume is 0.02 m^3, find the total thermal energy lost per minute when the alternating magnetic field operates at a frequency of 50 Hz.
solution_steps: Energy loss per unit volume per cycle (W) = 250 J/m^3.
Energy loss per cycle for the entire core = W * V = 250 * 0.02 = 5 Joules.
Frequency f = 50 Hz means 50 cycles per second. Number of cycles per minute = 50 * 60 = 3000 cycles.
Total energy loss per minute = Energy loss per cycle * Cycles per minute = 5 J * 3000 = 15000 Joules.

solved_numericals.question: In a transformer core, the hysteresis power loss is 400 W at a frequency of 50 Hz. Keeping the maximum flux density constant, what will be the hysteresis power loss when the frequency is increased to 60 Hz?
solution_steps: Hysteresis power loss is given by Steinmetz relation: P_h = eta f B_{max}^{1.6}.
Since B_{max} and the material constant eta remain constant, P_h is directly proportional to frequency f (P_h ∝ f).

solved_numericals.question: A sample of iron weighing 7.8 kg is subjected to an alternating magnetic field of frequency 50 Hz. If the density of iron is 7800 kg/m^3 and the hysteresis loop area corresponds to 300 J/m^3, calculate the annual hysteresis energy loss assuming continuous operation.
solution_steps: Volume of the iron sample V = Mass / Density = 7.8 kg / 7800 kg/m^3 = 0.001 m^3.
Energy loss per cycle for the sample = Loop Area * Volume = 300 J/m^3 * 0.001 m^3 = 0.3 J/cycle.
Power loss P_h = Energy loss per cycle * Frequency = 0.3 J * 50 s^{-1} = 15 W (Joules per second).
Total time in one year = 365 days * 24 hours/day * 3600 seconds/hour = 3.1536 * 10^7 seconds.
Total annual energy loss = Power * Time = 15 W * 3.1536 * 10^7 s = 4.73 * 10^8 Joules.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Quasi-static conditions are maintained during the tracing of the B-H loop, ignoring dynamic eddy current contributions at high frequencies.
Limitation: Steinmetz empirical power law (alpha approx 1.6) fails at extremely high magnetic induction values approaching magnetic saturation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Hysteresis loss depends only on the maximum magnetic field H.
common_misconceptions.correct: Hysteresis loss depends on the area of the B-H loop, which is determined by both the maximum field intensity and the magnetic properties (retentivity and coercivity) of the specific material.
common_misconceptions.why: Different materials subjected to the same maximum H will exhibit drastically different loop areas and energy losses.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Soft iron retains permanent magnetism permanently.
common_misconceptions.correct: Soft iron has low retentivity and very low coercivity, making it lose its magnetization easily once the external field is removed.
common_misconceptions.why: High coercivity and high retentivity (hard magnetic materials) are required for permanent magnets.

quick_revision: Hysteresis is the lagging of B behind H in a cyclic magnetization process.
Area of the B-H loop equals thermal energy dissipated per unit volume per cycle.
Retentivity is remaining B at H = 0; Coercivity is reverse H needed to make B = 0.
Soft magnetic materials have narrow loops and low losses, ideal for AC transformer cores.
Hard magnetic materials have wide loops and high coercivity, ideal for permanent magnets.
Steinmetz hysteresis power loss formula: P_h = eta f B_{max}^{1.6}.
